Two dimensions is a caricature. What happens with room to breathe? Training the same VAE at latent sizes \(L \in \{2, 8, 32, 128\}\) and looking at the per-dimension KL, i.e. how much information each latent dimension carries, reveals a most interesting observation.

At \(L = 128\), the model lights up roughly 30 dimensions and leaves the other ~98 at essentially zero KL. Given 128 dimensions, it refuses to use most of them. This is the information bottleneck from the rate objective in action. Each active dimension costs KL but must earn that cost by improving reconstruction, and once the ~30 dimensions MNIST genuinely needs are used, the rest are pure overhead and get driven to the prior. The model, thus chose its own dimensionality.

The numbers across the sweep tell the same story from another angle:

L test ELBO active units linear probe 2 −151 2 / 2 66% 8 −109 8 / 8 88% 32 −99 31 / 32 89% 128 −99 30 / 128 94%

The ELBO plateaus by \(L = 32\), a 4× bigger latent buys nothing more, because the model was already using only ~30 dimensions.

The Linear Probe

Though the VAE is a generative model and not a classifier, to measure its capabilities over MNIST, we trained a simple linear classifier. The linear probe is the accuracy of that linear classifier trained on the trained latent as well as over the raw MNIST pixels. At \(L = 2\) it sits below a 91% raw-pixel baseline signifying aggressive compression throwing away exactly the information we might have wanted for useful generation.

docs.title: Compression versus reconstruction: the β knob
docs.text:
We next use a weight, \(\beta\) on the KL term, which acts as a dial on the ELBO, tuning it between reconstruction and regularisation. Holding \(L = 32\) and sweeping \(\beta\) we trace out the rate–distortion curve, plotting rate \(R\) (the KL, the information pushed through the latent) against distortion \(D\) (the reconstruction cost), both in nats.

Every \(\beta\) is one operating point on a convex frontier. We cannot have both low rate and low distortion, and \(\beta\) chooses where we sit. The reconstructions across the same sweep make it visceral.

Small \(\beta\) gives sharp reconstructions; large \(\beta\) smears digits toward blurry averages as the latent is abandoned. The two endpoints are each instructive failures:

  • \(\beta = 0\) removes the KL brake entirely. Reconstruction is sharpest, but the latent now carries 634 nats ≈ 914 bits to represent a 784-bit image. That is expansion as opposed to compression. Without the KL penalty the encoder makes ultra-precise, prior-mismatched codes. From a Shannon standpoint we would do better sending the raw pixels.
  • \(\beta = 20\) over-penalises rate, and the latent collapses. Active units fall from 31 to 2, and the reconstructions become near-identical mush regardless of the input.

The useful representation lives at the knee. \(\beta = 1\) is exactly ELBO-optimal, compressing a 784-bit image down to about 30 nats of shared, generalisable structure.

This is where Shannon meets the ELBO

\(-\text{ELBO} = D + R\). The rate \(R\) is literally the channel rate through the latent (the bits we would spend transmitting the code) and \(D\) is the residual we must patch up afterwards. \(\beta\) trades one against the other.

docs.title: Watching features emerge
docs.text:
A final experiment, before we move on from VAEs. The 2D model was checkpointed on a log-spaced schedule, so we can replay the latent scatter across training and watch structure form across training epochs.

Surprisingly, emergence is not monotonic. 1 and 7, the most visually distinctive digits resolve at the very first epoch and stay put. They are the easy features, learned first. The crowded middle (0/2/3/5/6/8) starts as an undifferentiated blob and separates slowly and only partially. And 4 and 9 appear cleanly separated early, then re-entangle as training proceeds. An early, crude arrangement gets overwritten as the model optimises globally under the two-dimensional constraint, sacrificing the 4/9 split (cheap to give up, since they look alike) to make room for the harder digits.

If we only looked at the final epoch, we would conclude "4 and 9 overlap because they're similar". True, but we would miss that the model tried separating them and sacrificed them. Features form, drift, merge, and sometimes vanish. The training dynamics reorganise a representation rather than simply sharpening it.

docs.title: What a representation keeps
docs.text:
In conclusion, a VAE keeps the handful of shared factors that let it rebuild the data, about thirty dimensions' worth for MNIST and discards the per-instance detail as redundant. \(\beta\) sets how ruthless that discarding is, and the interesting representations sit at the knee between hoarding everything and collapsing to nothing.

The next question we attempt is whether a different objective, one with no reconstruction at all, keeps things different. That is the subject of the following post on self-supervised learning: no decoder, no pixels to rebuild, just the constraint that two views of an image should agree, evaluated, as here, with a linear probe on the frozen representation. The same yardstick, but a very different route.

docs.title: Self-Supervised Learning: Contrastive
docs.text:
With VAEs the question we asked was Can we compress the input into a latent representation that preserves enough information to reconstruct it? With self supervised learning we remove the reconstruction objective and instead ask Can we build a representation where different views of the same object are close together? In other words we are moving from focussing on how much information should the latent space contain to focussing on the nature of that information.

The central purpose of self-supervised representation learning is to train an encoder that extracts useful features from an image without requiring human-provided labels. The features, not the samples, are the product.

The basic idea is to take one image and generate multiple transformed views of it through cropping, blurring, colour jitter, flipping or similar augmentations. The pixels may change considerably, but the underlying image identity does not. A useful encoder should therefore produce representations that are stable under these transformations: different views of the same image should map to similar representations, while independent images should remain distinguishable.

The challenge though is representation collapse. If the only objective were to make two views of the same image similar, the encoder could map every image to the same constant vector. Every pair would then match perfectly, but the representation would carry no information whatsoever.

Every SSL method is a different answer to how do we avoid representation collapse?

docs.title: SimCLR: identify the matching view
docs.text:
SimCLR, the first method that we study, is a contrastive method. It prevents collapse by explicitly contrasting each image against the other images in the minibatch.

Reference

Chen, Kornblith, Norouzi & Hinton (2020), A Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations, ICML.

For every original image \(\mathbf{x}\), two random augmentations are drawn from a family \(\mathcal{T}\):

\[ \mathbf{x}_1 = t_1(\mathbf{x}), \qquad \mathbf{x}_2 = t_2(\mathbf{x}), \qquad t_1, t_2 \sim \mathcal{T} \]

Each view passes through the same two-stage neural network: an encoder \(f\), usually a convolutional network, and a projection head \(g\), usually a small multilayer perceptron.

graph LR
    X((x)) --> A1[Augmentation 1]
    X((x)) --> A2[Augmentation 2]

    A1 --> F1[Shared encoder f]
    A2 --> F2[Shared encoder f]

    F1 --> H1((h₁))
    F2 --> H2((h₂))

    H1 --> G1[Shared projector g]
    H2 --> G2[Shared projector g]

    G1 --> Z1((z₁))
    G2 --> Z2((z₂))

    Z1 --> L[Contrastive loss]
    Z2 --> L
    N[Other images in batch] --> L

The encoder produces \(\mathbf{h} = f(\mathbf{x})\) and the projector produces \(\mathbf{z} = g(\mathbf{h})\). The contrastive loss operates on \(\mathbf{z}\), while \(\mathbf{h}\) is retained as the representation for downstream applications.

For one anchor \(\mathbf{z}_i\), the loss asks the model to identify its corresponding view \(\mathbf{z}_j\) among all other views in the batch:

\[ \ell_{i,j} = -\log \frac{\exp \big( \text{sim}(\mathbf{z}_i, \mathbf{z}_j) / \tau \big)}{\sum_{k \neq i} \exp \big( \text{sim}(\mathbf{z}_i, \mathbf{z}_k) / \tau \big)} \]

where \(\text{sim}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{v} / (\|\mathbf{u}\| \|\mathbf{v}\|)\) is the cosine similarity and \(\tau\) is a temperature.

InfoNCE

This objective is the InfoNCE loss, which arises from noise-contrastive estimation. It is a softmax cross-entropy over a set of candidates in which the "correct class" is the matching view. Minimising it maximises a lower bound on the mutual information between the two views.

This is effectively a classification problem: which of the available representations is the other view of this image? The positive pair should have high similarity, while representations of independent images act as negatives.

If every input collapsed to the same vector, all similarities would be equal, the model could not identify the positive pair, and it would do no better than random guessing. Negatives therefore make total collapse incompatible with a low loss.

docs.title: Why separate the representation and the projection?
docs.text:
The contrastive objective encourages the model to suppress information affected by the augmentations. If colour jitter is used, for example, colour-sensitive information becomes inconvenient for the contrastive task. Applying that pressure directly to \(\mathbf{h}\) could cause the reusable representation to discard information that is still useful downstream.

The projection head provides a disposable training space:

\[ \mathbf{x} \longrightarrow \mathbf{h} \longrightarrow \mathbf{z} \]

The loss is evaluated on \(\mathbf{z}\), which allows the projector to specialise in augmentation invariance while giving the latent space \(\mathbf{h}\) room to remain richer. This separation is not mathematically guaranteed, since gradients still flow through both the projector and the encoder. But the architecture creates an inductive bias that lets the projector absorb some of the strongest pressure imposed by the objective.

After training, the projector is discarded and the encoder output \(\mathbf{h}\) is used.

docs.title: MoCo: a queue of historical negatives
docs.text:
SimCLR obtains its negatives from the current minibatch, so using more negatives normally requires a larger batch and more GPU memory. Momentum Contrast (MoCo) keeps the contrastive objective but changes how negatives are supplied. It introduces two separate paths: a query encoder and projector, and a key encoder and projector.

Reference

He, Fan, Wu, Xie & Girshick (2020), Momentum Contrast for Unsupervised Visual Representation Learning, CVPR.

graph LR
    X((x)) --> AQ[Query augmentation]
    X((x)) --> AK[Key augmentation]

    AQ --> FQ[Query encoder]
    FQ --> GQ[Query projector]
    GQ --> Q((q))

    AK --> FK[Key encoder]
    FK --> GK[Key projector]
    GK --> KP((k⁺))

    Q --> L[InfoNCE loss]
    KP --> L
    Queue[FIFO queue of historical keys] --> L

    FQ -. EMA .-> FK
    GQ -. EMA .-> GK
    KP --> Queue

For each image, the query is compared with one positive key generated from another view of the same image, and with a large queue \(\mathcal{Q}\) of keys generated from previous minibatches. The loss has the same broad form as SimCLR:

\[ \mathcal{L} = -\log \frac{\exp \big( \text{sim}(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{k}^+) / \tau \big)}{\exp \big( \text{sim}(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{k}^+) / \tau \big) + \sum_{\mathbf{k}^- \in \mathcal{Q}} \exp \big( \text{sim}(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{k}^-) / \tau \big)} \]

The query must identify its positive key among the queued negatives. The queue operates on a first-in, first-out basis: new keys are appended after each step and the oldest are dropped. This decouples the number of negatives from the minibatch size, so that

\[ \text{number of negatives} \approx \text{queue length} \]

rather than being tied to the batch size.

The query-side parameters \(\theta_q\) are optimised by backpropagation. The key-side parameters \(\theta_k\) receive no gradients; they are updated as an exponential moving average of the query-side parameters:

\[ \theta_k \leftarrow m \, \theta_k + (1 - m) \, \theta_q, \qquad m \in [0, 1) \]

The key encoder therefore changes slowly. This matters because the queue holds keys generated during earlier iterations, and a rapidly changing key encoder would make old and new keys mutually inconsistent. Momentum updating keeps the queued representations approximately compatible.

MoCo does not eliminate the need for negatives. It provides a memory-efficient way to maintain a great many of them. It can be considered an improved architecture but with the same mechanism as SimCLR.

docs.title: Inside SimCLR: What a Contrastive Objective Actually Learns
docs.text:
Having understood the theory behind contrastive self-supervised learning methods, we choose SimCLR, the simplest of these methods, to implement. The setup is a bigger step up from MNIST which we used for VAEs. CIFAR-10 is 60,000 real colour photographs: ten classes, 32×32 pixels and three channels. We train the SimCLR on this corpus and see how effectively it identifies features by using a linear probe as well as a k-NN classifier to measure discrimination before and after training.

Unlike the VAE, there is no reconstruction signal to lean on. No labels enter the training as well. The only training signal is: two augmented crops of the same photo should end up close together in representation space, and every other photo in the batch should end up far away. Hence the self-supervised.

docs.title: The setup
docs.text:
The primary encoder is a ResNet-18 with one deliberate adaptation. The standard ImageNet stem, a 7×7 stride-2 convolution followed by a stride-2 max-pool throws away most of a 32×32 image before the first residual block ever sees it, so it is swapped for a single 3×3 stride-1 convolution with no pooling. The rest is the usual four residual stages, ending in a 512-dimensional vector after global average pooling. That 512-D vector is the representation for everything that follows.

On top of it sits a small, disposable projector: Linear → BatchNorm → ReLU → Linear, 512 → 512 → 128 used only during training and thrown away afterwards. The contrastive loss is computed on the projector's 128-D output, not the primary's 512-D one, so that the pressure to discard augmentation-sensitive information (colour, if colour jitter is in the recipe) lands on the disposable projector rather than the representation we actually care about.

We train for 200 epochs, batch size 256, SGD with momentum and a cosine schedule with linear warm-up. As with the VAE, the model never sees labels during training. It appears to start off worse than the VAE, in fact, since photos sharing a class are also contrasted, with only crops coming from the same source image being 'labelled' as augmentations.

Collapse-proofing, and its sanity check

The trivial failure mode for this objective is mapping every image to the same constant vector. Every pair would then match perfectly. NT-Xent makes that solution actively bad: with equal representations, the "correct" positive is indistinguishable from every negative, and a 2N-way softmax over indistinguishable candidates scores \(\log(2N-1)\) nats, the worst value the loss can take, not the best. That is also the exact number the loss should read at random initialisation, since untrained embeddings point in roughly random directions. Ours came in at 6.231, against a predicted 6.236, a clean confirmation the wiring is right, the same role the ~540-nat check played for the VAE.

docs.title: The floor
docs.text:
Before training buys anything, how much does the architecture alone give away for free? A completely untrained, randomly-initialised primary still has convolutional structure such as local receptive fields and translation equivariance, so its features are not noise.

A linear probe on these random features reaches 37.9% (a ten-class problem, so chance is 10%), and a k-NN classifier reaches 28.6%. Diffuse, weakly separated, but not trivial. This is the number every trained method has to clear by a wide margin, exactly as the untrained VAE's ~543-nat reconstruction cost was the number training had to beat.

docs.title: Training, and a loss curve worth distrusting
docs.text:
NT-Xent drops sharply during the ten-epoch warm-up, then spends the remaining 190 epochs grinding down slowly from about 4.7 to 4.48, never getting close to zero, and looking almost flat for long stretches.

Why the loss looks flat while the model keeps improving

NT-Xent's floor is nowhere near zero. Even a perfect representation still has to win a genuinely hard 511-way classification every batch, so the loss saturates at some non-trivial value that has little to do with representation quality past a point. Over the stretch where our loss barely shifted from 4.70 to 4.48, the linear probe climbed from 77.9% to 88.1%, a ten-point gain in exactly the region the loss curve looks asleep. The loss is a training signal, not the yardstick; the probe is.

docs.title: Does it actually work?
docs.text:
random floor SimCLR, 200 epochs linear probe 37.9% 88.1% k-NN 28.6% 86.6%

More than double the floor on both metrics! A healthy, non-trivial result for this scale. Equally interesting is how the gap between those two metrics moved over the course of training:

epoch probe k-NN gap 1 53.7% 46.0% 7.8 pts 8 71.5% 64.4% 7.1 pts 32 77.9% 73.3% 4.6 pts 128 85.3% 82.4% 2.9 pts 200 88.1% 86.6% 1.6 pts Why does the k-NN gap close

A linear probe fits new weights to whatever the features look like, so it can always find some useful direction even in a fairly disorganised space. k-NN fits nothing. It just asks which training images are nearest in raw Euclidean distance, and that is only a good question once training has actually reshaped the geometry so that "nearby" means "similar." Watching the two metrics converge is a free, parameter-free signal that the representation is becoming genuinely organised, not just linearly decodable by an adaptive classifier.

docs.title: The scatter, before and after
docs.text:
Encoding the test set through the trained primary encoder and projecting to two dimensions with t-SNE gives the direct counterpart to the random-init picture above.

Ten classes, never named during training, falling into their own visibly separated regions purely from the constraint that crops of the same photo agree and crops of different photos disagree.

docs.title: The per-class picture
docs.text:
The aggregate numbers hide a nested classification worth pulling apart, since CIFAR-10's ten classes are not equally similar to each other. Four are vehicles, six are animals.

class accuracy most confused with automobile 96.8% truck (2.5%) truck 93.7% automobile (4.4%) ship 93.5% airplane (2.8%) airplane 92.5% ship (2.4%) frog 92.5% cat (2.6%) horse 89.8% deer (2.9%) deer 86.2% bird (4.2%) bird 80.9% deer (5.6%) dog 80.0% cat (13.3%) cat 75.4% dog (12.4%)

Two things stand out.

  1. Every single class's top confusion stays inside its own broad category. Vehicles get mistaken for other vehicles, animals for other animals, with not one cross-category error appearing as anyone's leading mistake. That structure was never trained for. It fell out of an objective that only ever asked "is this the same photo or not."

  2. One pair is a clear outlier. Cats and dogs confuse each other at 12–13%, three to five times the rate of every other pair, and tellingly, almost symmetrically in both directions. This is the CIFAR-10 analogue of the VAE's MNIST 4/9 tangle, and it does come with a caveat in favour of SimCLR. Cat-versus-dog is the notoriously hardest pair in CIFAR-10 for nearly every architecture ever thrown at it, contrastive or supervised, because the two classes share pose, indoor/outdoor context, texture, and scale far more than any other pair in the dataset.

docs.title: What a contrastive representation keeps
docs.text:
The VAE kept whatever a two-dimensional bottleneck needed to rebuild pixels i.e. a compressed, generative summary. SimCLR keeps whatever survives augmentation and still tells 512 numbers apart from 511 near-neighbours in a batch. It retains a discriminative summary, built with no reconstruction signal and no labels of any kind. Different objective, different mechanism, no decoder and yet the shape of what emerged rhymes pretty impressively. We obtained a clean separation for the visually distinctive classes, and one genuinely hard, symmetric tangle for the classes that legitimately look alike.

Other SSL paradigms like SimSiam and VICReg avoid collapse and aim to achieve similar discriminations through completely different mechanisms which we will explore next.

docs.title: Self-Supervised Learning: Non-contrastive
docs.text:
In SimCLR / MoCo and similar contrastive models, the model learns by pulling positive views together and pushing negative images apart. But why should learning useful representations require explicitly pushing different images apart?

Negatives introduce several problems:

  • performance depends heavily on how many negatives are available
  • large batches or queues are needed
  • some negatives may actually depict semantically similar things
  • the objective treats every other image as different, even when two images contain the same object class

For example, two different photographs of dogs are treated as negatives simply because they came from different source images. The contrastive loss pushes them apart, even though a useful semantic representation might ideally place them near one another.

So the non-contrastive question became:

Can we learn simply by making two views of the same image agree, without comparing them to other images?

And as with contrastive learning, the challenge again is representation collapse.

docs.title: BYOL: learning without negatives
docs.text:
Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL) asks whether useful representations can be learned without explicitly pushing independent images apart. It has two paths: an online path updated by gradient descent, and a target path updated through an exponential moving average.

Reference

Grill et al. (2020), Bootstrap Your Own Latent: A New Approach to Self-Supervised Learning, NeurIPS.

graph LR
    X((x)) --> A1[Augmentation 1]
    X((x)) --> A2[Augmentation 2]

    A1 --> FO[Online encoder]
    FO --> GO[Online projector]
    GO --> P[Predictor]
    P --> PO((p))

    A2 --> FT[Target encoder]
    FT --> GT[Target projector]
    GT --> ZT((z'))

    PO --> L[Matching loss]
    ZT --> SG[Stop-gradient]
    SG --> L

    FO -. EMA .-> FT
    GO -. EMA .-> GT

The online branch contains three learned modules, encoder \(\rightarrow\) projector \(\rightarrow\) predictor, while the target branch contains only encoder \(\rightarrow\) projector. The online prediction is trained to match the target projection:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{BYOL}} = \left\| \frac{\mathbf{p}}{\|\mathbf{p}\|_2} - \text{sg} \left( \frac{\mathbf{z}'}{\|\mathbf{z}'\|_2} \right) \right\|_2^2 \]

Here \(\text{sg}(\cdot)\) denotes stop-gradient: the target representation participates in the loss but is treated as a constant during backpropagation.

The same loss updates the online encoder, projector and predictor. The target encoder and projector are not updated by the loss; they slowly follow their online counterparts through an exponential moving average, exactly as in MoCo. The process can be read as a rapidly learning online network predicting the representation produced by a slowly moving target network.

Fresh augmentations are drawn at each training step, so over time the online network learns to predict representations that remain stable across many different views of each image.

BYOL's central surprise is that this works without negatives. Collapse is avoided through the asymmetry between the two branches. Stop-gradient prevents both sides from moving together within the same optimisation step, the predictor exists only on the online side, and the target network evolves slowly.

docs.title: SimSiam: stripping BYOL down to its essentials
docs.text:
SimSiam asks a natural follow-up question:

Is the momentum target network actually necessary?

BYOL contains several candidate anti-collapse mechanisms:

  • an online predictor
  • stop-gradient on the target branch
  • two separate parameter sets
  • an EMA target network

SimSiam removes the momentum encoder and shows that useful representations can still be learned. Both views now pass through the same shared encoder and projector.

Reference

Chen & He (2021), Exploring Simple Siamese Representation Learning, CVPR.

graph LR
    X((x)) --> A1[Augmentation 1]
    X((x)) --> A2[Augmentation 2]

    A1 --> F1[Shared encoder f]
    A2 --> F2[Shared encoder f]

    F1 --> G1[Shared projector g]
    F2 --> G2[Shared projector g]

    G1 --> Z1((z₁))
    G2 --> Z2((z₂))

    Z1 --> P1[Shared predictor q]
    Z2 --> P2[Shared predictor q]

    P1 --> L12[Match p₁ to sg z₂]
    Z2 --> SG2[Stop-gradient]
    SG2 --> L12

    P2 --> L21[Match p₂ to sg z₁]
    Z1 --> SG1[Stop-gradient]
    SG1 --> L21

The two branches share parameters:

\[ \mathbf{x}_1 \rightarrow f \rightarrow \mathbf{h}_1 \rightarrow g \rightarrow \mathbf{z}_1, \qquad \mathbf{x}_2 \rightarrow f \rightarrow \mathbf{h}_2 \rightarrow g \rightarrow \mathbf{z}_2 \]

and a predictor is applied to each projection, \(\mathbf{p}_1 = q(\mathbf{z}_1)\) and \(\mathbf{p}_2 = q(\mathbf{z}_2)\).

Training is symmetric in value but asymmetric in gradient flow. In one direction the prediction from view 1 is matched to the stopped projection from view 2, and in the other direction the roles switch:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{1 \rightarrow 2} = D \big( \mathbf{p}_1, \text{sg}(\mathbf{z}_2) \big), \qquad \mathcal{L}_{2 \rightarrow 1} = D \big( \mathbf{p}_2, \text{sg}(\mathbf{z}_1) \big) \]

The total loss averages the two:

\[ \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2} \big( \mathcal{L}_{1 \rightarrow 2} + \mathcal{L}_{2 \rightarrow 1} \big) \]

where \(D\) is typically the negative cosine similarity:

\[ D(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{z}) = - \frac{\mathbf{p}}{\|\mathbf{p}\|_2} \cdot \frac{\mathbf{z}}{\|\mathbf{z}\|_2} \]

docs.title: What stop-gradient changes
docs.text:
Consider the first direction, \(\mathbf{p}_1 \rightarrow \text{sg}(\mathbf{z}_2)\). The value of \(\mathbf{z}_2\) is used as the target, but no gradient flows through it, so within that loss term only the path producing \(\mathbf{p}_1\) is changed. For the reverse term the roles switch. Each branch therefore alternates between two roles:

  • predictor being optimised
  • fixed target for the other branch

The network is shared, but the gradient paths are not symmetric within each loss term.

docs.title: How this differs from BYOL
docs.text:
BYOL maintains two parameter sets:

Online network: updated by gradient descent
Target network: updated by EMA

SimSiam uses only one:

Shared network: updated by gradient descent
Target output:  detached for each directional loss

There is therefore no momentum encoder, no EMA update, no queue and no negatives. The architecture is much simpler, yet it still avoids collapse.

docs.title: What does SimSiam reveal?
docs.text:
SimSiam demonstrates that a slowly moving teacher is not essential. The critical structure is the asymmetric prediction problem created by a predictor on the optimised side and a stop-gradient on the target side.

It is slightly too strong to say that stop-gradient by itself prevents collapse. In the SimSiam architecture, removing stop-gradient causes collapse, and the predictor is also an important part of the successful configuration. The safer conclusion is that predictor asymmetry and stop-gradient are together sufficient to learn useful representations without negatives or a momentum target.

The theoretical explanation remains subtle. A collapsed representation is still mathematically compatible with the matching objective. It is the optimisation dynamics created by the stop-gradient and the predictor that steer training away from that solution. The resulting progression is:

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{BYOL} &= \text{predictor} + \text{stop-gradient} + \text{EMA target} \\ \text{SimSiam} &= \text{predictor} + \text{stop-gradient} \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Four answers to the same problem
docs.text:
These methods are best understood as different answers to one question: how can two views of the same image be made similar without mapping every image to the same representation?

Method Negatives Anti-collapse mechanism SimCLR in-batch contrastive loss over other images MoCo FIFO queue contrastive loss plus momentum key encoder BYOL none predictor, stop-gradient, EMA target SimSiam none predictor, stop-gradient

In every case the final product is the encoder representation \(\mathbf{h}\). The projection heads, predictors, queues and momentum networks are training mechanisms used to shape that representation, and they are discarded once self-supervised training is complete.

Evaluating a self-supervised encoder

The standard protocol is the linear probe: freeze the encoder, train a single linear classifier on \(\mathbf{h}\) using labelled data, and report its accuracy. A good self-supervised representation makes the classes linearly separable, so the quality of \(f\) can be measured without fine-tuning it.

docs.title: Inside SimSiam: What a Non-Contrastive Objective Learns, and How it Collapses
docs.text: SimCLR prevents representation collapse by contrasting with negatives. Every other image in the batch is actively pushed away, so mapping everything to one point makes the loss worse, not better. SimSiam does not rely on negatives at all. There is no queue, no momentum encoder, nothing pulling different images apart. Its only defence against collapse is architectural. A predictor on one branch, and a stop-gradient on the other. That seems like a decidedly weaker safety net. Does it actually work? And what happens if we take the safety net away?

docs.title: The setup
docs.text:
We have the same primary encoder as SimCLR in the CIFAR-adapted ResNet-18 with a 512-D output, the same augmentation pipeline, same CIFAR-10 data, same batch size (256) and optimiser (SGD, cosine schedule with warm-up), deliberately matched so the only thing that differs between the two experiments is the anti-collapse mechanism itself.

On top of the primary sits a 3-layer projector (Linear → BN → ReLU, twice, then a final Linear → BN with no learnable affine parameters, a specific detail from the original paper's own implementation) and a 2-layer bottleneck predictor (Linear → BN → ReLU → Linear, 128 → 64 → 128). The loss is symmetrised negative cosine similarity: each branch's prediction is matched against the other branch's target, with the target detached from the graph so no gradient flows back into it.

\[ \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\big[D(p_1, \operatorname{sg}(z_2)) + D(p_2, \operatorname{sg}(z_1))\big], \qquad D(p, z) = -\frac{p}{\lVert p\rVert}\cdot\frac{z}{\lVert z\rVert} \]

That sg (stop-gradient) is the entire collapse prevention mechanism.

A different init check, on purpose

NT-Xent's random-init value was \(\log(2N-1)\), a large positive number, the worst possible score, which is what makes contrastive collapse structurally impossible. SimSiam's loss is bounded in \([-1, 1]\), and at init, with \(p\) and \(z\) pointing in roughly random directions, cosine similarity concentrates near zero. So the expected value is close to 0, not the worst score on the scale. Ours read 0.085. A loss near its floor at init doesn't mean anything is wrong here, but it does mean the loss alone will never be enough to distinguish a healthy run from a broken one.

docs.title: Does it actually match SimCLR?
docs.text:
random floor SimCLR, 200 epochs SimSiam, 200 epochs linear probe 37.9% 88.1% 86.6% k-NN 28.6% 86.6% 85.0%

Within a point and a half of SimCLR on both metrics, with an objective that never compares one image to another. This is pretty much what we expected going in. A non-contrastive mechanism isn't a better answer to collapse than a contrastive one, just a different one, so parity rather than a clear win is the honest prediction. It's still impressive though! An objective that never explicitly says "these two images are different" produces a representation that separates ten classes almost as well as one that does, purely from getting the optimisation dynamics right.

docs.title: Comparison at a granular level
docs.text:
The aggregate numbers being close is one thing. The per-class breakdown paints an even more congruous picture.

class SimCLR accuracy SimSiam accuracy automobile 96.8% 97.0% truck 93.7% 94.0% ship 93.5% 94.6% airplane 92.5% 90.6% frog 92.5% 91.6% horse 89.8% 89.4% deer 86.2% 86.0% bird 80.9% 77.0% dog 80.0% 75.2% cat 75.4% 70.7%

Almost the identical ranking, class for class, from two objectives that share no design principle. In both runs, independently, every single class's top confusion stays inside its own broad category. Vehicles only ever get mistaken for other vehicles, animals only for other animals. And in both runs the single hardest pair is the same one: cats and dogs, confused with each other three to five times more often than any other pair, and confused almost symmetrically in each direction (SimCLR: 12.4% / 13.3%; SimSiam: 13.2% / 15.3%).

Two mechanisms that don't agree on how to prevent collapse arrived at the same picture of what's easy and what's hard. That's evidence the structure being found here is a property of the data, of how visually similar CIFAR-10's classes genuinely are to each other rather than an artefact of either training procedure.

docs.title: What SimCLR couldn't show us: Collapse
docs.text:
SimCLR structurally cannot collapse. Mapping every image to the same vector makes the negatives-based loss worse, so gradient descent is pushed away from that solution automatically. SimSiam's non-collapse isn't loss-driven at all. It's a side effect of the stop-gradient asymmetry, which means it is possible, on purpose, to remove it and watch the trivial solution win.

Doing that exposes something interesting: the loss cannot tell you when this has gone wrong.

epoch healthy loss broken loss (no stop-gradient) 1 −0.60 −0.80 2 −0.75 −0.98 4 −0.70 −0.98 8 −0.76 −0.98 16 −0.82 −0.99

Both curves are deeply negative by epoch 16. If anything, the broken run's loss looks more converged. Watching only the loss, this run would read as a clean success, arguably a better one than the healthy run, since it's closer to the theoretical floor of −1.

The number that actually tells the story is the effective rank of the representation i.e. how many of the primary's 512 output dimensions carry independent information, measured as \((\sum \lambda_i)^2 / \sum \lambda_i^2\) over the covariance eigenvalues \(\lambda_i\). It is bounded in \([1, 512]\). 1 means every image maps to (almost) the same vector, 512 means all 512 dimensions carry equal, independent variance.

Why not just threshold the raw variance?

The obvious first attempt to count dimensions whose raw variance across the dataset exceeds some cutoff turns out to fail here for two compounding reasons. First, a cosine-similarity loss is invariant to the overall magnitude of the primary's output, so weight decay steadily shrinks that magnitude over hundreds of epochs with nothing anchoring it, driving every dimension's raw variance toward zero even while the representation's direction, the only thing the loss and the linear probe actually use, stays fully informative. Second, and more fundamentally, a fixed threshold doesn't generalise across dimensionality at all: a healthy, isotropically-spread 512-D vector has roughly \(1/512\) of its variance in each individual dimension purely from being spread over 512 directions, comfortably under any threshold calibrated for a much lower-dimensional space. The eigenvalue ratio above sidesteps both problems at once, multiplying every feature by a constant leaves the ratio exactly unchanged, and it needs no threshold to calibrate in the first place.

Healthy SimSiam's effective rank, checked at epoch 200 turns out to be 31.1 out of 512. Not maximally spread, but nowhere near collapsed, and in a similar ballpark to the ~30 active dimensions the VAE found useful for a completely different dataset and objective, a resonance worth noting without over-reading into. The broken run, with the stop-gradient removed:

epoch 1 2 4 8 16 20 effective rank 1.19 1.24 1.07 1.52 1.00 1.03

Pinned at the collapsed end of the scale from the very first epoch onward. Two objectives with loss curves that look, if anything, more converged than the healthy run's but with a representation that never escaped total collapse.

docs.title: Worse than doing nothing at all
docs.text:
The linear probe over the same run tells the sharpest version of this story:

\[ 40.5\% \rightarrow 41.6\% \rightarrow 36.2\% \rightarrow 34.4\% \rightarrow 30.0\% \rightarrow \mathbf{29.4\%} \]

Not flat but declining. And the final number, 29.4% linear probe / 25.3% k-NN, sits below the completely untrained, random-initialisation floor of 37.9% / 28.6% from the very first experiment in this series. Twenty epochs without the stop-gradient didn't just fail to learn, they actively destroyed the crude signal a random network already provided for free, because once the target branch stops holding still, minimising the loss and minimising usefulness point in the same direction.

The per-class picture confirms the failure is structural. In the healthy runs, confusion was localised with nearly every class under 5%, with cat/dog as the one clear exception, and the vehicle/animal boundary held without a single crossing. In the collapsed run, every class shows substantial confusion (12% to 27%), and that boundary breaks down too: horse's top confusion becomes truck (19.1%), an animal mistaken for a vehicle, something that never happened across either healthy run. Collapse doesn't just erode fine-grained accuracy, it erases the coarse structure underneath it as well.

docs.title: A second, independent way to break it
docs.text:
Removing the stop-gradient isn't the only way to collapse SimSiam. The predictor exists specifically to give the "predicting" branch a role the target branch doesn't share. Swap it for the identity function (\(p = z\)) and that asymmetry disappears too, even with the stop-gradient still in place.

This ablation starts from a worse position than the first one. Even a completely untrained primary produces highly correlated outputs for different random images, a known signal-propagation artefact of deep, untrained CNNs, unrelated to SimSiam itself. So with no predictor to break that symmetry, the loss sits close to its collapsed value before a single gradient step is taken.

epoch 1 2 4 8 16 20 effective rank 1.04 1.04 1.17 1.34 1.15 1.08

Pinned even tighter to the collapsed floor than the stop-gradient ablation was, from the very first checkpoint onward. Final numbers: 33.8% linear probe, 27.8% k-NN which is again below the untrained random floor, a representation actively made worse than doing nothing at all.

The per-class picture adds two more findings:

  1. One specific confusion recurs in both: horse's top confusion is truck in the stop-gradient ablation, and it's truck again here. Two unrelated ways of breaking the same model landed on the exact same cross-category mistake. Perhaps whatever faint residual signal survives total collapse in either failure mode may be tracking something crude like colour or outdoor-background statistics, similar enough between horses and trucks to survive even when everything else is destroyed.

  2. This run's aggregate accuracy (33.8%) is higher than the stop-gradient ablation's (29.4%), but its coarse category structure is more broken. Two cross-superclass confusions here (bird → airplane joins horse → truck) against only one in the other ablation. Aggregate accuracy and structural integrity are not the same axis. A collapsed representation can claw back a point or two of raw accuracy by spreading its one surviving direction a little more evenly across classes, while simultaneously losing more of the coarse boundary that both healthy runs preserved without a single exception. Reading only the headline probe number would rank this run as the less damaged one; the per-class picture says the opposite.

docs.title: What the experiment teaches
docs.text:
SimCLR and SimSiam land in the same place by two unrelated routes, genuine evidence that what's being discovered is a fact about the data, not a quirk of either method. But only SimSiam can be taken apart to show why it works. Pull out either half of the asymmetry that prevents collapse, the stop-gradient or the predictor and a representation that matched SimCLR almost point for point collapses to a single effective dimension, while its training loss still seems to insist that everything is fine both times. The representation-space diagnostic if it disagrees with the loss curve, is the metric to trust.

Representational learning, particularly VICReg is the next to observe, and it gets its own version of this experiment. Rather than an architectural asymmetry, its anti-collapse mechanism is an explicit variance term in the loss, and it can be broken just as directly. Zero out that one term and watch the same story play out.

docs.title: Self-Supervised Learning: Regularising the Latent Space
docs.text:
Previously we have framed self-supervised learning as a set of different answers to one problem: how to make two views of an image agree without mapping every image to the same constant vector i.e. prevent representation collapse. Contrastive methods (SimCLR, MoCo) answered from the sample side, using negatives to force independent images apart. Non-contrastive methods (BYOL, SimSiam) answered from the optimisation side, using a predictor and stop-gradient to make collapse dynamically unreachable. Barlow Twins and VICReg are a third family, and their answer is the most direct of the three: constrain the statistics of the latent space so that a collapsed representation is explicitly penalised.

The earlier families avoid collapse indirectly, through what you compare against, or through how gradients flow. Regularisation methods instead write down what a healthy latent space should look like and add it straight to the loss:

Views of the same image should agree, latent dimensions should stay active, and different dimensions should carry different information.

The architecture is the plainest among all the SSLs. Both views pass through the same encoder and projector with no predictor, no momentum encoder, no queue and no negatives. Everything distinctive lives in the loss, which is computed over the statistics of a batch of embeddings.

graph LR
    X((x)) --> A1[Augmentation 1]
    X((x)) --> A2[Augmentation 2]

    A1 --> F1[Shared encoder f]
    A2 --> F2[Shared encoder f]

    F1 --> G1[Shared projector g]
    F2 --> G2[Shared projector g]

    G1 --> ZA((z_A))
    G2 --> ZB((z_B))

    ZA --> S[Loss on batch statistics]
    ZB --> S

docs.title: Barlow Twins: make the cross-correlation matrix \(I\)
docs.text:
Barlow Twins draws two augmented views \(x_A = t_A(x)\) and \(x_B = t_B(x)\), embeds both to \(z_A, z_B\), and, after standardising each embedding dimension along the batch, computes the cross-correlation matrix between the dimensions of the two views:

Reference

Zbontar, Jing, Misra, LeCun & Deny (2021), Barlow Twins: Self-Supervised Learning via Redundancy Reduction, ICML.

\[ C_{ij} = \frac{\sum_b z^A_{b,i}\, z^B_{b,j}}{\sqrt{\sum_b (z^A_{b,i})^2}\;\sqrt{\sum_b (z^B_{b,j})^2}} \]

\(C\) is a \(d \times d\) matrix indexed by embedding dimensions (not samples), with every entry in \([-1, 1]\). The loss simply asks \(C\) to become the identity:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{BT} = \sum_i (1 - C_{ii})^2 + \lambda \sum_{i \neq j} C_{ij}^2 \]

The two terms carry the whole idea:

  • Diagonal, \((1 - C_{ii})^2\) → invariance: Pushing \(C_{ii}\) towards 1 means dimension \(i\) of view A and dimension \(i\) of view B are perfectly correlated: the two transformations of the same image produce the same latent, dimension by dimension.
  • Off-diagonal, \(C_{ij}^2\) for \(i \neq j\) → redundancy reduction: Driving these to zero decorrelates the latent dimensions from one another, so different dimensions are pushed to encode different information.

docs.title: Why this prevents collapse
docs.text:
If every image mapped to the same vector, the embedding dimensions would become highly correlated with each other, and the off-diagonal terms of \(C\) would be large, not zero. Collapse and \(C = I\) are incompatible, so the objective penalises collapse directly, without ever needing a negative example. Barlow Twins is not trying to make different images orthogonal (that is the contrastive idea). It is trying to make the two views agree and the latent dimensions decorrelate.

Decorrelation is not the same as activity

Barlow Twins encourages dimensions to be uncorrelated, but it does not explicitly demand that each dimension carry a minimum variance. It is best read as "make the latent dimensions decorrelated and view-invariant" rather than "force every dimension to be active." That stronger, more explicit requirement is exactly what VICReg adds.

docs.title: VICReg: variance, invariance, covariance
docs.text:
VICReg (Variance-Invariance-Covariance Regularisation) makes the anti-collapse mechanism fully explicit by splitting it into three named terms applied to the batch of embeddings.

Reference

Bardes, Ponce & LeCun (2022), VICReg: Variance-Invariance-Covariance Regularization for Self-Supervised Learning, ICLR.

  • Invariance: the usual SSL objective, that two views agree:
\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{inv}} = \tfrac{1}{N}\sum_b \lVert z^A_b - z^B_b \rVert^2 \]
  • Variance: the most explicit anti-collapse component. For each dimension, compute its standard deviation across the batch and penalise it with a hinge whenever it falls below a target \(\gamma\):
\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{var}} = \tfrac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d} \max\!\big(0,\; \gamma - \operatorname{std}(z_{\cdot, j})\big) \]

This says, in effect: no dimension is allowed to go quiet.

Dimension 1: active       OK
Dimension 2: active       OK
Dimension 3: collapsed    penalised
  • Covariance: decorrelate the dimensions (the same job as Barlow's off-diagonal term), by penalising the off-diagonal entries of the embedding covariance matrix:
\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{cov}} = \tfrac{1}{d}\sum_{i \neq j} \big[\operatorname{Cov}(z)\big]_{ij}^2 \]

The variance and covariance terms are applied to each branch separately; invariance couples the two branches. The total loss is a weighted sum:

\[ \mathcal{L} = \lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{inv}} + \mu\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{var}} + \nu\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{cov}} \]

The conceptual advance over Barlow Twins is the variance term. Barlow decorrelates dimensions but does not directly insist each one stays alive; VICReg's hinge makes "every dimension carries a minimum of information" a first-class, explicit constraint.

docs.title: Three families, three sides of the same problem
docs.text:
Placing all three families side by side, the distinction is where each one attacks collapse:

Family Methods Where collapse is prevented Contrastive SimCLR, MoCo sample side: negatives push independent images apart Non-contrastive BYOL, SimSiam optimisation side: predictor + stop-gradient (+ EMA) Regularisation Barlow Twins, VICReg latent-space side: direct statistical constraints on the embeddings

The regularisation view is appealing because it names the target. Rather than hoping that negatives or optimisation dynamics induce a good latent space, it defines one (invariant, active, non-redundant) and optimises for it.

docs.title: The connection back to VAEs
docs.text:
This is where the SSL story loops back to the VAE. A VAE can suffer posterior collapse: latent dimensions stop carrying information about the input, their variance across the data drops to near zero, and they become inactive. In the VAE experiments, that showed up concretely: given 128 latent dimensions, the model used only about 30 and left the rest at essentially zero KL. There, low per-dimension variance was a diagnostic, something you measure after training to see how much capacity the model actually used.

VICReg takes that very diagnostic:

\[ \operatorname{Var}(z_j) \]

and moves it inside the loss. What the VAE leaves to chance (and you check for afterwards), VICReg forbids by construction.

VAE:          latent collapse is possible; you diagnose it after training.
Barlow Twins: redundant latent dimensions are penalised.
VICReg:       inactive dimensions are directly penalised,
              and redundant dimensions are discouraged.

Barlow Twins and VICReg move self-supervised learning away from preventing collapse indirectly (through negatives or optimisation tricks) and instead impose direct statistical constraints on the latent space, so that representations are kept invariant, active, and non-redundant by the objective itself.

docs.title: Inside VICReg: Preventing Collapse by Writing the Constraint Down
docs.text: SimCLR prevents collapse by actively pushing away every other image in the batch. SimSiam removes the negatives and survives on architectural asymmetry alone, with a predictor on one branch and a stop-gradient on the other. VICReg removes the architecture too and focusses inwards onto the representation. Both branches here are perfectly symmetric. No predictor, no stop-gradient, no negatives of any kind. Collapse is prevented by punishing any latent dimension whose variance across the batch drops too low. If the first two methods each found an implicit way to avoid collapse, this one explicitly writes the constraint down. Does saying it out loud work better, or differently, than relying on negatives or asymmetry?

docs.title: The setup
docs.text:
We use the same primary encoder as the other two: the CIFAR-adapted ResNet-18 with a 512-D output, same augmentation pipeline, same CIFAR-10 data, same batch size (256) and optimiser (SGD, cosine schedule with warm-up), deliberately matched so the only thing that differs across all three experiments is the anti-collapse mechanism itself.

On top sits a wide expander, the opposite shape from SimCLR's compressing projector or SimSiam's bottleneck predictor: Linear(512,2048) → BN → ReLU → Linear(2048,2048) → BN → ReLU → Linear(2048,2048), deliberately ending on a plain, unnormalised Linear layer.

Why the last layer has no batch norm

If the final layer were normalised the way SimSiam's projector deliberately is, that normalisation would satisfy the variance term structurally regardless of what the loss is doing, making the variance weight vacuous no matter what it's set to. The loss needs to act on genuinely unconstrained outputs for the constraint it enforces to mean anything at all.

The loss has three independent terms, computed on each branch and averaged:

\[ \mathcal{L} = \lambda \cdot \operatorname{MSE}(z_1, z_2) \;+\; \mu \cdot frac12 ig[h(z_1) + h(z_2) ig] \;+\; u \cdot frac12 ig[c(z_1) + c(z_2) ig] \] \[ h(z) = rac{1}{D}\sum_{j=1}^{D} \max\! ig(0,\ \gamma - \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(z_j) + \epsilon}\, ig), \qquad c(z) = rac{1}{D}\sum_{i eq j} C_{ij}^{\,2},\quad C = rac{1}{N-1} ilde z^{ op} ilde z \]

with the paper's own weights kept unchanged: \(\lambda = \mu = 25\), \( u = 1\), \(\gamma = 1\). Invariance is plain MSE with no normalisation anywhere. Unlike SimCLR/SimSiam's cosine-based losses, this term alone would happily reward shrinking both views toward a single point, since a smaller gap between them reduces MSE regardless of overall scale. Variance is the actual anti-collapse mechanism. Hinge every dimension's per-batch standard deviation against a floor \(\gamma\), independently on each branch. A dimension whose spread drops below the floor is directly penalised, full stop; nothing else in this loss cares whether a magnitude collapse happens, so this term alone is carrying that entire load. Covariance discourages different dimensions from carrying redundant information, penalising the off-diagonal entries of the batch covariance matrix.

A different init check, on purpose

NT-Xent's random-init value was \(\log(2N-1)\), a large, predictable number. SimSiam's bounded loss concentrated near 0. VICReg's MSE-based invariance term has no comparable universal target. Its value at init depends on the untrained network's raw, unconstrained output scale, which isn't pinned to anything. So the init check here doesn't assert a number; it just confirms all three terms come back finite and non-negative before training starts. Not every method offers a clean invariant to check against, and pretending otherwise would be manufacturing a number rather than reporting one.

docs.title: Training: two curves that don't do what you'd guess
docs.text:
Watching inv, var, and cov separately over 200 epochs turns up two things that aren't the obvious first guess.

var declines the entire run, from 0.685 at epoch 1 down to 0.339 at epoch 200, but it never gets close to the floor of zero the hinge is aiming for. Even at epoch 200, the weighted variance term (\(\mu \times 0.339 \approx 8.5\)) is still the single largest contributor to the total loss (13.7), ahead of both invariance and covariance combined. The constraint is never fully satisfied; the optimiser settles into an equilibrium where it's still being actively paid for, all the way to the end.

cov, meanwhile, rises across the run, from 0.819 to 2.952, despite being the term whose entire job is to push it down. The resolution is that raw covariance isn't the same thing as correlation: \(\operatorname{Cov}(z_i, z_j) = \rho_{ij}\,\sigma_i\sigma_j\). As the variance term pushes every dimension's standard deviation up toward its floor, the whole representation's scale grows, and a shrinking correlation coefficient can still produce a larger raw covariance number if the per-dimension scale is growing faster than the correlation is falling. The scale-invariant read is the one to trust here, exactly the lesson the VAE's active-units metric and SimSiam's effective-rank fix both already taught: participation ratio climbs cleanly to 86.3/512 across the same run, confirming the representation really is becoming more decorrelated relative to its own scale, even while the raw number moves the "wrong" way.

docs.title: Does it actually work?
docs.text:
random floor SimCLR SimSiam VICReg linear probe 37.9% 88.1% 86.6% 86.5% k-NN 28.6% 86.6% 85.0% 86.0% effective rank n/a n/a 31.1/512 86.3/512

A third mechanism, sharing no design principle with the other two, lands within a point and a half of both on accuracy. The pattern holds a third time: negatives, architectural asymmetry, and an explicit loss constraint all arrive at essentially the same representation quality.

The rank number is the interesting new one. VICReg's representation spreads its variance across nearly three times as many effective dimensions as SimSiam's, for statistically indistinguishable classification accuracy. This as a matter of fact, falls directly out of what the loss optimises for. Participation ratio measures two things: how evenly variance is spread across dimensions, and how decorrelated those dimensions are from each other. VICReg's variance and covariance terms are a direct, explicit pressure toward precisely that. SimCLR's negatives act on images, not dimensions; SimSiam's asymmetry has no notion of "dimension" at all. Neither has any mechanism that cares how the 512 dimensions individually behave, only that the whole vector avoids collapsing as one. VICReg is the only one of the three whose objective is, in effect, partially the same computation as the diagnostic. That the extra spread buys no extra accuracy is itself quite noteworthy. Roughly 30 well-organised dimensions are already enough to solve this classification task, and the other ~56 VICReg finds room for are decorrelated but functionally redundant for it.

docs.title: The per-class picture
docs.text:
class SimCLR SimSiam VICReg automobile 96.8% 97.0% 95.7% ship 93.5% 94.6% 93.7% truck 93.7% 94.0% 92.8% frog 92.5% 91.6% 91.4% airplane 92.5% 90.6% 90.5% horse 89.8% 89.4% 88.6% deer 86.2% 86.0% 85.4% bird 80.9% 77.0% 80.1% dog 80.0% 75.2% 75.2% cat 75.4% 70.7% 71.4%

Three findings, and none of them are new exactly, they're the same two findings from the SimCLR/SimSiam comparison, confirmed a third time by a mechanism that shares nothing with either.

  1. The ranking rhymes. Vehicles and frog/airplane above 90%, horse/deer in the mid-80s, bird/dog/cat at the bottom: the same clustering, three unrelated objectives running.
  2. The vehicle/animal boundary holds without exception. Every class's top confusion (airplane↔ship, automobile↔truck, bird↔deer, cat↔dog, deer↔bird, dog↔cat, frog→cat, horse→deer) stays inside its own broad category. Zero cross-superclass errors, for the third time running.
  3. Cat and dog are the hardest pair a third time, and the dog→cat figure (15.4%) lands almost exactly on SimSiam's (15.3%).

docs.title: Breaking it: zero out the variance term
docs.text:
SimSiam's break-it experiment needed a structural change (removing the stop-gradient, or swapping the predictor for the identity) because its anti-collapse mechanism is a piece of architecture. VICReg's equivalent needs no special flag: the variance term already has a continuous weight, so --var-weight 0.0 on the ordinary training script is the ablation.

epoch loss inv var cov 1 0.507 0.0159 0.951 0.109 2 0.0013 5.3e-5 0.989 6.2e-7 4 0.0012 4.8e-5 0.989 3.7e-6 8 1.9e-4 7.6e-6 0.990 2.3e-7 16 8.1e-7 3.2e-8 0.990 4.4e-14 20 5.7e-7 2.3e-8 0.990 2.1e-14

This is a different kind of failure than SimSiam's. SimSiam's broken loss converged toward its bounded floor of \(-1\), a finite number that could plausibly look like real convergence. Here, with the variance floor gone, mapping every image to the same output vector makes inv trivially zero, and with zero variance across the batch there's nothing left to covary, so cov collapses to zero too. Both surviving terms have their literal global minimum exactly at total collapse, so this isn't a loss that merely looks converged: it mathematically is the correct answer to a now-degenerate objective, and it gets there inside two epochs.

The variance term's own floor, confirmed to four decimal places

With var_weight=0, the variance term is excluded from the gradient entirely, so it's a pure bystander here, free to just report what happened. It converges to 0.98999..., and that number isn't arbitrary. Total collapse drives every dimension's variance to exactly zero, so the hinge's own numerical floor sets its value at \(\gamma - \sqrt{\epsilon} = 1 - \sqrt{10^{-4}} = 0.99\) exactly. The math and the observed number agree to four decimal places: direct, quantitative confirmation that the collapse is total, not partial.

epoch probe k-NN effective rank 1 37.6% 32.8% 1.33 2 36.6% 32.2% 1.14 4 36.3% 30.7% 1.26 8 36.5% 31.6% 1.68 16 35.0% 30.1% 1.75 20 34.7% 30.4% 1.75

Rank pinned near 1 for the entire run, probe sitting below the random floor (37.9%) throughout, kNN hovering just above its own floor (28.6%), a clearly, thoroughly collapsed representation, in the same territory as both SimSiam ablations (final ranks 1.03 and 1.08).

But it fails quietly, unlike SimSiam whose broken runs kept producing real, if harmful, gradients for the full 20 epochs, since its loss stays bounded but non-zero, training kept actively eroding the representation the whole way (its stop-gradient ablation's probe fell from 40.5% at epoch 1 to 29.4% by epoch 20). Here, once inv and cov hit essentially zero around epoch 2, there is no more loss signal left to act on. participation_ratio barely moves after that (1.14 → 1.26 → 1.68 → 1.75), despite the learning-rate schedule still ramping toward its peak. The representation free-falls to the trivial solution almost immediately, then the network is effectively frozen there rather than being dragged progressively further down.

That difference shows up sharply in the per-class breakdown:

class accuracy most confused with frog 48.6% deer (13.1%) ship 46.4% airplane (13.4%) automobile 42.0% truck (15.7%) truck 41.1% automobile (16.1%) airplane 40.4% ship (20.2%) dog 31.4% frog (15.7%) horse 30.1% dog (13.8%) deer 30.0% frog (24.7%) bird 19.9% deer (19.0%) cat 17.3% frog (19.8%)

Every single top confusion here still stays inside its own broad category, vehicles confused only with vehicles, animals only with animals: the same boundary the three healthy runs preserved without exception. That is the opposite of what happened to SimSiam: both of its ablations broke that boundary (horse→truck appeared in both, bird→airplane in one), an animal-for-vehicle mistake that never occurred in any healthy run of any method. VICReg's collapsed representation, despite being just as numerically dead by every aggregate metric, never makes that particular kind of mistake.

The likely explanation is the same "quiet death" mechanism above. SimSiam's ablations kept a live, non-zero loss actively reshaping the representation for the entire 20 epochs, which is plausibly what it took to corrupt even the coarse structure. VICReg's ablation collapses to a literal near-zero loss within two epochs and then stops moving in any meaningful sense, closer to a network that free-fell partway and was caught than one that was actively driven somewhere worse for twenty epochs straight.

docs.title: What the experiment teaches
docs.text:
Three anti-collapse mechanisms that share no design principle all land within a point and a half of each other on accuracy, all agree on which classes are easy and which are hard, and all preserve the exact same vehicle/animal boundary without exception. That triple agreement is strong evidence the structure being found is a fact about CIFAR-10, not an artefact of any one method.

But the three mechanisms disagree completely on how they fail once broken. SimCLR structurally cannot collapse at all. SimSiam's collapse is architecturally driven and stays live for as long as training continues, actively eroding the representation until even the coarse category boundary gives way. VICReg's collapse is near-instant and then goes numerically silent, a representation that is dead by every quantitative measure yet, oddly, still respects the one piece of structure every healthy run agreed on. Collapse, it turns out, is not a single failure mode. It's as varied as the mechanisms built to prevent it.

I-JEPA, the predictive family, is next, and it gets to answer a different question entirely: what happens when the pressure to avoid collapse comes not from negatives, asymmetry, or an explicit constraint, but from predicting representations directly.

docs.title: Confidence Audit: Do Language Models Know When They're Wrong?
docs.text:
Ask a language model any question today and you can expect an answer. Ask it how sure it is and you promptly get a confidence score. Both seem convincing and LLMs seem to know what they are doing. But does that number mean anything? Can a model tell the answers it got right from the ones it got wrong? Accuracy doesn't tell you that. A model that is right 80% of the time and exudes "95% confidence" every time is a usable answerer but a poor judge of itself. Here we audit that second skill across nine models, 680 questions and seven ways of asking for confidence, and find that what a model says about its confidence and what its behaviour reveals are two quite different things.

Most language models have become adept at answering questions convincingly. With reasoning models going through several stages and iterations, the accuracy of their answers have increased. But models, both the vanilla ones and the more sophisticated reasoning ones, hallucinate.

docs.title: Hallucination as a confidence problem
docs.text:
In Why Language Models Hallucinate, Kalai et al. explain a hallucination as a plausible but false statement made by a model. Hallucinations according to them, are not a mysterious glitch but a statistical consequence of how models are built. Pre-training makes some errors unavoidable, especially on singleton facts that appear rarely in the training data, but which the model is still forced to accommodate due to binary classification pressures. Post-training then optimises models for test-taking benchmarks that score a right answer as 1 and both a wrong answer and an "I don't know" as 0. Under that grading, guessing always beats admitting uncertainty, so a model learns to answer confidently whether or not it knows.

That makes hallucination as much about confidence as about accuracy. A wrong answer flagged as uncertain is one a user, or a system built around the model, can check. The same wrong answer delivered with full confidence is the one that does the damage. But what about reasoning models?

Thinking before answering raises accuracy, sometimes dramatically, but it does not follow that a model knows better when it is still wrong. In Reasoning about Uncertainty: Do Reasoning Models Know When They Don't Know? Mei et al. found that reasoning models typically state 85% confidence or more even on answers they get wrong, and that on those wrong answers they grow more overconfident the longer they reason. Zeng et al. in Thinking Out Loud: Do Reasoning Models Know When They're Right? found that reasoning training improves calibration on reasoning-heavy tasks but much less consistently on factual questions, where open reasoning models say "I don't know" far less often than ordinary instruction-tuned ones.

Pre-trained base models are naturally well-calibrated because they are optimised using cross-entropy loss. But reasoning models undergo post-training with methods like RLHF and instruction tuning which are often incentivised for confidence by their human rewarders, thereby losing their base calibration. Another intuition: a chain of thought builds an argument for its answer, and the argument persuades the model that wrote it as much as the reader. That is what leads to autoregressive stubbornness where a mistake made in an earlier stage of reasoning is justified and compounded further down the chain. The audit includes one model with thinking on and off, on the same weights, to test this directly.

docs.title: What we build on
docs.text:
We base this study on other works that try to tackle the confidence measurement problem.

  • ConfidenceBench (ffrench-Constant et al., 2026) extracts verbal confidence from 15 frontier models on 200 multiple-choice questions in four categories, one of them unknowable, scored with Brier. It found that the most accurate model is not the best calibrated, but it reports no results per category. Grading self-knowledge separately for each kind of question, with difficulty held fixed, is what this audit adds.
  • ForecastBench (Karger et al., 2024). Questions about events that had not happened when the models were trained, so the answers cannot have been memorised. The audit's forecasting questions come from its question sets.

The other confidence signals in the audit, agreement across a model's own samples and the probability it puts on its answer tokens, are standard measures from the wider calibration literature.

The audit is built from the test side. Rather than one overall calibration score, which can hide a model that is overconfident on obscure facts and underconfident on arithmetic, we sort questions by what it takes to answer them, give each kind a difficulty dial, and grade self-knowledge separately on each.

docs.title: The questions
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Q[680 questions] --> R[Has a right answer]
    Q --> N[Has a right behaviour]
    Q --> F[Has an outcome]
    R --> R1["Recall<br/>Who wrote X?<br/>dial: how famous X is"]
    R --> R2["Computation<br/>What is 2139 × 7874?<br/>dial: number of digits"]
    R --> R3["Perception<br/>Spell 'dialogue' backwards<br/>dial: word length"]
    N --> N1["False premise<br/>When did Kafka write When I Have Fears?<br/>right: correct the premise"]
    N --> N2["Ambiguous title<br/>Who directed The Rescue?<br/>right: ask which one"]
    N --> N3["Unknowable<br/>Who will be President of France in 2079?<br/>right: say it can't be known"]
    F --> F1["Forecast<br/>75 markets resolved after every model's cutoff<br/>scored against what happened"]

The three answerable categories are each 150 questions, 30 at each of five difficulty levels, and they are chosen because they fail for different reasons. Recall fails when a fact is rare in the training data. Computation fails when errors pile up digit by digit during generation. Perception fails because a model sees tokens, not letters, so counting the n's in "recommendations" is a blind spot it may not know it has. The dials do their job: accuracy falls level by level for every model, from near 100% to near 0.

docs.title: Seven ways of asking "how sure are you?"
docs.text:
Every question goes to every model in sixteen separate calls, each a fresh conversation, so the methods can be compared question by question.

flowchart LR
    Q[One question] --> P["P: just answer<br/>(+ token probabilities: E)"]
    Q --> B["B: answer 10 more times at T=1<br/>how many agree with P?"]
    Q --> A["A: answer, then give confidence"]
    Q --> D["D: give confidence, then answer"]
    Q --> C["C: answer only if more than t sure<br/>wrong costs t/(1-t), t = 0, .5, .75, .9"]

Two of these are things the model says (A after answering, D before it, a feeling-of-knowing). Two are things it does: whether its own samples agree (B) and how much probability it puts on its answer tokens (E, where the provider exposes them). The last (C) states the stakes in the prompt, using the scoring rule Kalai et al. proposed in Why Language Models Hallucinate: under it, answering only pays when you are more than t sure, so a model that knows its own confidence should abstain more as t rises.

The nine configurations were picked to exercise the methods rather than to rank vendors:

Model Where What it tests Qwen3-1.7B, 8B, 14B local RTX 4090 size within one family, every method including E Qwen3-8B, thinking on local RTX 4090 reasoning on vs off, same weights Qwen3-8B-Base local RTX 4090 base vs instruct (few-shot; P, B, E only) GPT-4o, Grok 4.1 Fast Azure AI Foundry other vendors, with token probabilities GPT-5 nano Azure AI Foundry a closed reasoning model, no token probabilities Claude Haiku 5.5 Anthropic API no temperature control, no token probabilities

The whole thing came to about 100,000 model calls and under $7: about $5.80 on Foundry, $0.30 for Claude, and the 4090's electricity.

docs.title: Grading without fooling ourselves
docs.text:
Arithmetic and spelling can be marked by code. "Who wrote X?" mostly can too, by matching against known aliases. But "did this response correct the false premise?" needs a judge, and the first judge we tried (Qwen3-14B) agreed with a hand-labelled set only 77 times out of 120. It stumbled on bare refusals like "Unknown" and on denials that happened to contain a year.

flowchart LR
    R[Response] --> Rules{"Code rules<br/>exact answer, alias,<br/>bare refusal"}
    Rules -- decided --> L[Label]
    Rules -- not decided --> J["Judge: Qwen3-14B<br/>thinking off,<br/>rubric with examples"]
    J --> L
    G["Gold set: 120 hand labels<br/>+ 88 blind held-out"] -. checks .-> Rules
    G -. checks .-> J

So we built the grader the other way round: code rules for everything they can decide, the judge only for the rest, and both checked against hand labels. Claude drafted 120 labels, which were reviewed by hand, and the rubrics were rewritten until rules plus judge agreed on 114. Then came the honest test: two blind held-out sets, labelled with the judge's answer hidden.

Thinking off was the better judge

Letting the judge reason before labelling scored 112/120 against 114 with thinking off. Among its new mistakes: it marked "Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross" wrong as the composers of The Social Network, a score the two of them wrote. On the API models' held-out set, all five disagreements had the judge stricter than the hand label, so if anything the scores below understate the models.

docs.title: Two kinds of self-knowledge
docs.text:
Before getting into the results, there is one distinction that helps us on how to read them. The standard measure of whether confidence separates right from wrong is AUROC, the chance that a randomly chosen right answer carries more confidence than a randomly chosen wrong one (0.5 is a coin toss, 1.0 is perfect). But a model can score well on it by knowing only that long multiplications are risky and short ones are safe. That's real self-knowledge, but coarse. The finer skill is knowing which of several equally hard answers is the wrong one.

Within-level AUROC keeps only the second kind, by comparing right and wrong answers only inside the same difficulty level.

Parallels with human metacognition research

The corresponding tool from human metacognition research, meta-d′, (see A signal detection theoretic approach for estimating metacognitive sensitivity from confidence ratings,) needs a two-choice task to measure against; open-ended answers don't have one, so we control for difficulty this way instead, plus a regression with a separate baseline for every model × category × level.

docs.title: What they say vs what they do
docs.text:
Here is the main result in one picture: within-level AUROC for every model, category and method.

Read it by column. The two "said" columns (A and D) are informative on recall and drift to 0.5, no information at all, on computation and perception. The two "done" columns (B and E) stay well above 0.5 almost everywhere. Grok's token probabilities are the exception, saturated near certainty on everything.

The same split shows up in calibration. Take one set of weights, Qwen3-8B, and read its confidence three ways:

Its stated confidence is a single dot: nearly every answer is stated at 0.9 or more, whether the accuracy behind it is 20% or 40%. Its sample agreement is a proper curve, if an overconfident one. And the base model, before any instruction tuning, sits close to the diagonal on recall, which is exactly what Kalai et al. predict: pre-training produces calibrated probabilities, and post-training erodes them.

The practical upshot is a simple rule. When a model says it is sure but its own samples scatter, believe the samples:

What that looks like

Grok 4.1 Fast, asked What is 2139 × 7874? (16,842,486) three separate times, answered 16,834,486, then 16,843,086, then 16,845,186, each time with confidence 1.0. Only 2 of its 10 samples agreed with its first answer. GPT-4o, asked who wrote the screenplay for the Kannada film Kotigobba, named K. S. Ravikumar at confidence 0.9; 3 of 10 samples agreed, and the answer was wrong.

docs.title: The category matters, not just the difficulty
docs.text:
Is perception just harder? The regression says no. With a separate baseline for every model × category × level cell, the slope tells how much more likely a model's most confident answer is to be right than its least confident one, at the same difficulty:

Perception sits below recall for every method, and for the two stated methods its slope is indistinguishable from zero. Plotting every cell at its own accuracy shows the same thing without the model: at matched accuracy, stated confidence works on recall and is flat on perception, while sample agreement keeps working on both.

That fits the mechanism. A model has some internal sense of how familiar a fact is; it has no view at all of the letters inside a token, so it cannot know that it has miscounted them.

docs.title: The hard-easy effect, but only in the words
docs.text:
Psychologists have long seen people overconfident on hard questions and underconfident on easy ones (see Lichtenstein, S. & Fischhoff, B. Do those who know more also know more about how much they know?). The models show half of it, the former half.

GPT-4o's stated confidence (blue) sits at 1.0 on the hardest multiplications, where it is right 0% of the time. It looks calibrated on easy questions only because it happens to be right there; there is no underconfidence on the easy end, just a line pinned at the top. Its sample agreement (green) and token probability (yellow) fall with accuracy. The base model's lines follow accuracy almost exactly. GPT-5 nano is the one model that errs the other way: it is nearly always right on computation and perception, and still says about 0.8.

docs.title: Thinking on: more right, not more aware
docs.text:
Qwen3-8B with thinking on and off is the same weights answering the same questions, so the pair isolates what reasoning does. It transforms accuracy where the answer can be worked out: computation goes from 34% right to 100%, perception from 23% to 89%, and the model corrects 68% of false premises instead of 15%. On facts it helps far less, 34% right against 25%, because no amount of reasoning recovers a fact the model doesn't hold.

Those facts are where the overconfidence shows. After thinking, the probability the model puts on its final answer averages 0.95 on recall questions it gets right only a third of the time; without thinking, the same measure averaged 0.39. The reasoning settles on an answer and the answer is then written out with near certainty, so the token probability loses most of its signal: within-level AUROC 0.57, against 0.81 without thinking. Stated confidence after thinking is also high, 0.88 on average at 32% right, although it separates right from wrong a little better than without thinking (0.78 against 0.66), and so does sample agreement (0.90 against 0.77). On computation thinking leaves no errors to measure, so the test of its self-knowledge rests on facts and spelling.

docs.title: Before or after answering?
docs.text:
Is confidence more honest before the model commits to an answer, a feeling of knowing, than after, when it has an answer to defend? On the same questions, within levels:

There is no general winner. Asking first helps Qwen3-8B and GPT-4o on computation, hurts Qwen3-14B, and on recall asking after is as good or better. An early version of this analysis said "before beats after on computation"; that turned out to be mostly the coarse kind of self-knowledge, knowing which levels are hard, and it largely vanished within levels.

Claude Haiku shows its work

Asked for an answer plus a confidence in JSON, Claude Haiku 5.5 often ignored "Reply with only a JSON object" and worked the problem out first: 777 × 933 = 777×900 + 777×33 = 699300 + 25641 = 724941, then the JSON. That lifts its accuracy and means its "before" confidence on arithmetic isn't really before. Those replies are flagged and left out of this comparison.

docs.title: Questions without a proper answer
docs.text:
Unknowable questions are easy for everyone. False premises and ambiguous titles are where the models separate, and Claude Haiku is in a class of its own: it corrects every false premise and asks which work is meant on three ambiguous titles in four ("Ambiguous: several films are titled 'The Rescue.'").
